title: Chronic pain in European adult populations: a systematic review of prevalence and associated clinical features
authors: Caroline Rometsch; Alexandra Martin; Florian Junne; Fiammetta Cosci
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain in European adults, assessed as point, period, and lifetime prevalence across body locations including headaches, neck/shoulder, back, abdomen, hip, arm/wrist/ankle, leg/knee, chest/stomach, and lower extremities.
context_note: European adult general population; prevalence data from EU countries including Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, The Netherlands, and United Kingdom, with many missing countries.
bps_function_set: intervention rationale; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS only in the abstract and discussion to justify comprehensive, multimodal care. The review itself stratifies prevalence by sociodemographic and clinical features and conducts meta-regression on sex, marital status, and employment, not as variables in a BPS model.
integration_mechanism_summary: No three-domain mechanism is proposed. The only named mediator is pain interference linking CP severity to affect and quality of life; otherwise domains are associated, listed, or used to justify comprehensive care.
quality_assessment_tools_1: joanna biggs institutes' critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (jbi)
emergent_labels_4: International Association for the Study of Pain
emergent_labels_7: Joanna Biggs Institutes' Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data (JBI)
conceptual_tensions_1: The review invokes a comprehensive BPS model but does not define it or use it to select, measure, or model variables
conceptual_tensions_2: Prevalence heterogeneity is attributed to diagnostic criteria, cutoffs, and assessment tools, yet these sources of variation are not modeled
conceptual_tensions_3: Narrative associations between sociodemographic features and CP are not statistically significant in meta-regression
conceptual_tensions_4: European coverage is uneven, with many countries explicitly listed as missing despite the review's European scope
conceptual_tensions_5: The discussion broadens from BPS to psychosomatic medicine, clinimetrics, macro-analysis, and Whipple's principle without resolving the BPS operational gap
additional_observations_1: The meta-regression operationalizes sociodemographic moderators only as sex, marital status, and employment status
additional_observations_2: Quality assessment focused on prevalence-study methods rather than BPS construct validity
additional_observations_3: SF-36 was the only named patient-reported outcome instrument in the evidence
additional_observations_4: Psychosomatic medicine, clinimetrics, macro-analysis, and Whipple's principle extend the care rationale beyond BPS
additional_observations_5: Environmental factors are named but not operationalized
additional_observations_6: Pain location and regional pain burden are the main biological operationalization
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS only as a rationale for comprehensive, multimodal care after a prevalence-focused synthesis. It names biological, psychological, and social correlates but treats them mainly as associated features, with no substantive three-domain model or measured BPS variables.
coding_rationale: Multifactorial: all domains are named, but BPS is used mainly for care recommendations. Triadic integration is descriptive only; no three-domain mechanism is modeled.

title: Chronic pain in European adult populations: a systematic review of prevalence and associated clinical features
authors: Caroline Rometsch; Alexandra Martin; Florian Junne; Fiammetta Cosci
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain in European adult populations
context_note: European adult populations across multiple countries
bps_function_set: background framing; justification; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The BPS model is invoked as a justification for comprehensive, multicomponent care approaches but is not formally defined or operationalized. The review uses BPS language to frame the need for interdisciplinary treatment without specifying mechanisms or integrating domains analytically.
conceptual_tensions_1: BPS label used to justify multicomponent care without defining or integrating the three domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Psychological constructs mentioned (depression, anxiety, catastrophizing) but not defined or theoretically integrated
conceptual_tensions_3: Domains listed as interacting in discussion but no specific mechanisms or pathways proposed
additional_observations_1: The review focuses on epidemiology and associated factors rather than theoretical integration
additional_observations_2: No formal definition of the biopsychosocial model is provided
additional_observations_3: Psychological constructs are operationalized through association with CP rather than theoretical framework
additional_observations_4: Social factors are treated as demographic variables rather than systemic influences
synthesis_note: This review uses the biopsychosocial label to justify comprehensive care approaches for chronic pain but does not operationalize or integrate the three domains. Biological, psychological, and social factors are mentioned as associated variables with CP prevalence, but no mechanisms or pathways linking them are proposed. The BPS model serves as a rhetorical label for multicomponent treatment rather than an analytical framework.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial because all three domains are mentioned as associated factors, but integration is none because no mechanisms or pathways are proposed. The review is an epidemiological synthesis that uses BPS language to justify comprehensive care without substantive integration.
